title: CW procedures, prosigns and Q signals
blurb: Use full break-in, read the common Q signals and prosigns, and answer a CQ at the right speed and frequency.

G2C01.why: **Full break-in (QSK)** lets you receive **between code characters and elements**, so you can hear interruptions.
G2C01.trap: BK is a prosign. Full break-in is about the receiver gaps, not the key type.

G2C02.why: **QRS?** asks you to **send slower**. S for slow.
G2C02.trap: QRQ is the opposite, send faster.

G2C03.why: **KN** means you are **listening only for the named station(s)**. Others should not call.
G2C03.trap: SK, not KN, ends a contact.

G2C04.why: **QRL?** asks **"are you busy?" or "is this frequency in use?"**. Ask it before you call.

G2C05.why: Answer at **your comfortable copy speed, but no faster than the CQ**. The caller chose a speed they can copy.
G2C05.trap: No fixed 5 or 10 wpm calling speed applies.

G2C06.why: **Zero beat** means matching your transmit frequency to the received signal's frequency.
G2C06.trap: It's about frequency, not speed or split operation.

G2C07.why: A **C** after the RST report means a **chirpy** (unstable) signal.
G2C07.trap: Key clicks have their own suffix, K.

G2C08.why: **AR** marks the **end of a formal message**.
G2C08.trap: SK ends a contact, BK means break, KN limits who may reply.

G2C09.why: **QSL** means **I have received and understood**. A QSL card confirms a contact.

G2C10.why: **QRN** means **I am troubled by static**. N for noise.
G2C10.trap: QRM is interference from other stations.
